title: The Six-Card Cover Problem: a computer-assisted determination of g(6)
description:
The case r = 6 of the Erdős–Lovász cover number problem: the question, posed in 1974 in the paper that introduced the local lemma, of the minimum number of edges g(r) in an r-uniform intersecting hypergraph with cover number r. The exact values known are g(3) = 6, g(4) = 9 and g(5) = 13; the strongest published general lower bound gives g(6) ≥ 14.

A reproducible computer-assisted determination of g(6), the smallest number of blocks in a pairwise intersecting 6-uniform family whose transversal number is 6.

The lower bound is reached in two stages. Families of at most fifteen cards are excluded by two independent routes: a weighted counting inequality with thirteen degree histograms, and a stronger eleven-card lemma stating that every pairwise intersecting 6-uniform family of eleven cards has a four-element transversal. Sixteen cards are then excluded by a finite reduction to 463 canonical eight-card cores; every associated CNF instance is unsatisfiable, and every unsatisfiability carries a DRAT certificate accepted by an independent proof checker. The upper bound is an explicit seventeen-card family on 27 symbols for which all 136 pairs intersect and none of the 80,730 five-symbol subsets is a transversal. Hence g(6) = 17.

The archive contains four papers and an overview, the enumeration and verification scripts, the canonical core data, the reduction data, SAT run records, the certificate summary, three representative CNF/DRAT pairs, and an independent re-verification log recording what was re-run and what remains a reading obligation.

DRAT certification removes the SAT solver from the trusted base. It does not establish that the reduction reaches every counterexample, nor that the encoding means what the mathematics means; both are named as open obligations in the text.

Status. Research draft. No priority is claimed. The lower bound is computer-assisted and has not been independently reviewed by a human referee or a proof assistant: DRAT certification removes the SAT solver from the trusted base, but the completeness of the finite reduction and the faithfulness of the CNF encoding remain open obligations that no certificate discharges. The upper bound is an explicit witness and is checkable directly. AI tools (ChatGPT, OpenAI; Claude, Anthropic) were used throughout the work and its review; every number reported is regenerated by a script or certified by a proof file in the archive.

The full certificate archive is not in this record. This deposit carries the repository only. The complete set of 463 CNF files and 463 DRAT proofs, with the per-core checker output and verification markers, is about 534 MB and is published as the release asset g6-certificates-463.zip at github.com/Osman209/g6-equals-17/releases. The three hardest instances ship inside this deposit in data/cnf/, so the certification step can be reproduced without it.
